Fit a latent class model

Source: R/lpa.R
lca.Rd

Latent class analysis describes heterogeneity in categorical response patterns through a specified number of latent classes. Each class is characterized by the probabilities of the response categories for each indicator. These probabilities describe how response patterns differ between classes.

lca() estimates the class-specific response probabilities and class proportions, together with posterior membership probabilities for each observation. Indicators are assumed independent conditional on class membership unless associations between selected indicators are explicitly specified. The posterior probabilities describe uncertainty in classification; an observation's assigned class is a summary of these probabilities.

The model treats observations as independent. For observations nested within groups, use multilca(). Ordinal and count indicators can also be fitted using the structured measurement models described in multilpa().

Usage

lca(data, vars, n_classes, ...)

Arguments

data

A data frame with one row per observation.

vars

Names of the discrete indicator columns. Categories are taken from the data. Columns named in ordinal or count (through ...) are modelled as such; the rest are categorical.

n_classes

Number of classes; a positive integer.

...

Further arguments for multilca(), such as missing, n_starts, seed, min_probability and profile_covariates, except id and n_group_classes.

Value

A fitted object as returned by multilca(), usually of class multilpa, or multilpa_covariates with membership covariates. Its call records the original lca() call. Classes are labelled profile_1, profile_2, and so on in the returned tables.

Conditions

latents_bad_argument when id, n_group_classes or n_profiles is passed; the conditions multilca() raises otherwise.

References

Lazarsfeld, P. F., & Henry, N. W. (1968). Latent Structure Analysis. Houghton Mifflin.

See also

lpa() for continuous indicators; multilca() for the two-level model; enumerate_lca() to compare numbers of classes.

Examples

fit <- lca(student_esm, c("time_with_friends", "on_social_media",
                          "tv_video_games", "sports"),
           n_classes = 2, n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
fit
#> Latent class analysis: 2 classes
#> 2582 observations; 4 categorical indicators
#> Classes are labelled profile_1, profile_2, ... in every table.
#> Log likelihood: -4560.239231 | AIC: 9138.478 | BIC: 9191.185
#> Converged: TRUE | iterations: 69 | best log likelihood reached by 3 of 3 starts (3 converged)
#> 
#> Class sizes   profile_1 35.6% (919)   profile_2 64.4% (1663)
#> 
#> Response probabilities
#>          indicator category profile_1 profile_2
#>  time_with_friends       no     0.782     0.897
#>  time_with_friends      yes     0.218     0.103
#>    on_social_media       no     1.000     0.552
#>    on_social_media      yes     0.000     0.448
#>     tv_video_games       no     1.000     0.670
#>     tv_video_games      yes     0.000     0.330
#>             sports       no     0.902     0.943
#>             sports      yes     0.098     0.057
#> 
#> Thresholds and standard errors: get_results(x, "responses").
#> Every other table: get_results(x, what = ), or get_results(x, "all").
plot(fit, what = "heatmap")
